Among the ducks of the genus Anas, the Mexican duck (Anas diazi) exhibits life-history traits that reflect its semi-arid, highland habitat. Reproductive output is characterized by a single annual clutch, with females laying ten eggs per nest [N_R_i = ten eggs per nest], and this clutch frequency of one per year [F_R_i = clutch frequency of one per year] represents the maximum observed reproductive rate for the species. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg, which correlates closely with subsequent offspring quality, averages 43 grams [Ww0 = 43 grams], though individual egg masses can range from roughly 27 to 41 grams depending on maternal condition and food availability during yolk formation. This investment in relatively large eggs is thought to enhance hatchling survival in the unpredictable wetland environments the species frequents across the interior highlands of Mexico and the southwestern United States.

Incubation under parental care occurs at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a thermal regime that synchronizes embryonic development over approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days]. This developmental period, while typical for a dabbling duck of this body size, is at the upper end of the reported range for the species, which can extend from 23 to 30 days depending on local ambient conditions and nest attentiveness. Upon hatching, the wet weight at birth of a neonate chick is recorded at 31.8 grams [Wwb = 31.8 grams], a value that reflects the nearly complete absorption of yolk reserves and the rapid transition to exogenous feeding under the watchful supervision of the hen. The downy young are highly precocial and capable of leaving the nest within hours of hatching, though they remain dependent on the mother for brooding and guidance as they learn to forage in shallow marsh edges.

The post-hatching growth trajectory of Anas diazi is rapid, and chicks achieve the developmental milestone of fledging at a comparatively early age. Under favorable conditions, young birds attain full flight capability at 52 days after hatching [tx = 52 days after hatching], a timing that aligns well with the onset of the monsoon season in their native range, when pond productivity peaks and invertebrate prey becomes abundant. This fledging age is followed by a substantial period of somatic growth and social learning before individuals transition into the adult population. During this extended juvenile phase, body mass increases steadily, and the ultimate wet weight for adult females, measured just prior to egg-laying when body condition is at its annual peak, reaches 1200 grams [Wwi = 1200 grams]. Notably, female mass fluctuates considerably over the course of the year, declining after incubation and molting before being rebuilt during the winter foraging period.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs after a considerable delay relative to the completion of structural growth. Puberty is reached at 156 days after hatching [tp = 156 days after hatching], meaning that birds hatched in the early summer attain full gonadal development by winter's end, though they typically do not breed until their second calendar year. The time since birth at first brood, marking the initiation of reproductive activity, is observed at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a timeline that confines successful reproduction to individuals that have survived at least one full annual cycle. This pattern of deferred breeding is common among waterfowl with limited seasonal windows for nesting, as it allows younger birds ample opportunity to acquire the body reserves and territorial experience necessary for successful incubation and brood rearing.

Longevity records for the Mexican duck in the wild are limited, but available data from banding studies indicate that the maximum lifespan can reach 21.3 years [am = 21.3 years]. This value, which converts to roughly 7,775 days, places Anas diazi among the longer-lived dabbling ducks, a trait that is likely linked to its comparatively low annual fecundity and the high survival demands of its arid, ephemeral wetland habitats. Such an extended lifespan provides multiple opportunities for reproduction across successive years, partially compensating for the modest single-clutch strategy. The interplay between a moderate reproductive rate, a protracted juvenile period, and considerable adult longevity shapes a life history that is well adapted to the environmental stochasticity of the North American desert and grassland regions where this species has evolved.
